publication_info: Topic-level synthesis focused on representative works since 2024. Core papers include OVAM by Pablo Marcos-Manchon, Roberto Alcover-Couso, Juan C. SanMiguel, and Jose M. Martinez (CVPR 2024; VPULab/Autonomous University of Madrid and University of Barcelona; https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.14291), REPA by Sihyun Yu, Sangkyung Kwak, Huiwon Jang, Jongheon Jeong, Jonathan Huang, Jinwoo Shin, and Saining Xie (ICLR 2025 oral; KAIST, Korea University, Scaled Foundations, NYU; https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.06940), ConceptAttention by Alec Helbling, Tuna Han Salih Meral, Ben Hoover, Pinar Yanardag, and Duen Horng Chau (ICML 2025 oral; https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.04320), U-REPA by Yuchuan Tian, Hanting Chen, Mengyu Zheng, Yuchen Liang, Chao Xu, and Yunhe Wang (NeurIPS 2025; https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.18414), and Mustafar / Towards Multimodal Understanding via Stable Diffusion as a Task-Aware Feature Extractor by Vatsal Agarwal, Matthew Gwilliam, Gefen Kohavi, Eshan Verma, Daniel Ulbricht, and Abhinav Shrivastava (arXiv preprint submitted July 9, 2025; University of Maryland and Apple; https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.07106). Supporting feature-extraction evidence also comes from Not All Diffusion Model Activations Have Been Evaluated as Discriminative Features (https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.03558), Three Things We Need to Know About Transferring Stable Diffusion to Visual Dense Prediction Tasks (ECCV 2024), and DIFT / Emergent Correspondence from Image Diffusion (NeurIPS 2023; https://diffusionfeatures.github.io/).
code_and_model_availability: Public code is broadly available for the main building blocks: OVAM at https://github.com/vpulab/ovam, ConceptAttention at https://github.com/helblazer811/ConceptAttention, REPA at https://github.com/sihyun-yu/REPA, U-REPA at https://github.com/YuchuanTian/U-REPA, DIFT at the project page https://diffusionfeatures.github.io/, and diffssl at https://github.com/soumik-kanad/diffssl. Mustafar exposes a public project page (https://vatsalag99.github.io/mustafar/) but states GitHub is coming soon, so code availability for the CLIP-fusion variant is incomplete.
core_hypothesis: The central hypothesis is that diffusion models learn structured internal states that are often more spatially precise, more compositional, and more text-grounded than standard CLIP embeddings. Instead of using diffusion only as a generator, these works treat U-Net or DiT hidden states, attention queries, attention outputs, latent trajectories, and open-vocabulary attention maps as transferable supervision. When these signals are aligned with or fused into CLIP-like pipelines, they can repair known CLIP weaknesses in region grounding, attribute binding, viewpoint reasoning, and fine-grained visual discrimination.
problem_setting: The target weakness is not generic image semantics but the specific failure mode of global contrastive encoders: CLIP often compresses semantically similar yet visually distinct images into nearby embeddings, struggles with region-level localization, underperforms on spatial and compositional reasoning, and can miss subtle parts, actions, or attributes needed for vision-centric tasks. Diffusion features are studied as auxiliary representations because their denoising process preserves multi-scale spatial structure while text conditioning injects concept-specific alignment signals throughout the backbone.
relation_to_clip_training: Most papers in this route do not re-pretrain CLIP from scratch. The dominant pattern is to keep the diffusion backbone frozen and either fuse its features with a CLIP-based stack, compare against CLIP baselines, or use diffusion attention maps as dense supervision for open-vocabulary tasks. Direct end-to-end distillation into a standalone CLIP encoder exists more as a design opportunity than as a mature standard recipe [uncertain].
diffusion_role: Diffusion acts mainly as a frozen feature extractor and dense region supervisor. OVAM uses Stable Diffusion cross-attention as an open-vocabulary attribution engine; ConceptAttention repurposes DiT attention layers as saliency-producing concept encoders; Mustafar uses Stable Diffusion as a task-aware visual encoder and fuses it with CLIP features; DIFT and related work treat denoising activations as transferable dense descriptors; REPA and U-REPA show that diffusion hidden states are semantically alignable to strong vision encoders, which supports the idea that these hidden states are valid representation-transfer targets.
diffusion_backbone_family: The literature spans latent diffusion U-Nets and newer multi-modal diffusion transformers. Stable Diffusion v1.5, v2.1, and SDXL dominate the U-Net branch, typically with a VAE latent space and CLIP-based text conditioning. ConceptAttention studies Flux-style multi-modal DiTs and references SD3-style architectures, while REPA targets DiT and SiT families and U-REPA extends alignment to canonical U-Nets. The common theme is that auxiliary representations are extracted from denoisers rather than from final generated pixels.
signal_extraction_protocol: The signal protocol is highly specific and usually layer- and timestep-sensitive. OVAM extracts pixel queries from U-Net cross-attention blocks and recombines them with keys from an attribution prompt, then aggregates attention maps across blocks, timesteps, and heads. Mustafar inspects Stable Diffusion v2.1 features from cross-attention queries, attention outputs, and residual outputs, with strong results from up-stage blocks such as U-L1-R1-B0-Cross-Q and early-to-mid timesteps around t=10 to t=100; it also studies averaged cross-attention maps for text grounding. ConceptAttention injects concept tokens into Flux MMAttn layers, updates them with one-directional cross-plus-self attention, and computes saliency by dot-producting image output vectors with concept output vectors in the attention output space; it uses activations from the last 10 of 18 MMAttn layers. REPA aligns projected noisy hidden states to pretrained encoder features, while U-REPA aligns U-Net middle-stage features after MLP projection and upsampling, augmented by a manifold regularizer. The broader activation survey in arXiv:2410.03558 explicitly argues that queries, keys, output vectors, and embedded ViT activations should all be considered candidate discriminative features.
generator_adaptation_strategy: For auxiliary-representation use, the diffusion backbone is usually frozen or almost frozen. OVAM is training-free apart from lightweight optimization of text-token embeddings; ConceptAttention requires no extra training; Mustafar uses a frozen Stable Diffusion v2.1 feature extractor and trains only the projection/fusion stack around it; DIFT-style pipelines are also extraction-first. REPA and U-REPA are the exception in that they modify the diffusion training objective itself, but even there the external encoder used for alignment is frozen.
clip_backbone_and_component: The CLIP side is usually a baseline visual encoder or a fusion partner rather than the only optimized network. In Mustafar, CLIP-style visual features from a LLaVA-v1.5 pipeline are fused with diffusion features either by concatenation or by cross-attention, where CLIP features act as queries and diffusion features act as keys and values. In the broader route, CLIP also appears as the text-conditioning module native to Stable Diffusion, as a comparison baseline for segmentation and image-text matching, and as an optional teacher family in REPA implementations. Direct, large-scale updating of the CLIP image encoder itself is still limited in the cited papers [uncertain].
transfer_mechanism: Three transfer mechanisms dominate. First, feature fusion: conditional or unconditional diffusion features are concatenated with CLIP-style tokens or injected through cross-attention, as in Mustafar. Second, dense alignment: cross-attention maps or output-space concept maps are used as region-level semantic supervision, as in OVAM and ConceptAttention. Third, representation matching: projected diffusion hidden states are explicitly aligned to strong pretrained visual encoders via similarity losses, as in REPA and U-REPA. Across these mechanisms, diffusion contributes localized structure and prompt-aware semantics that CLIP alone tends to underrepresent.
training_objectives: Objective design varies by subproblem. OVAM optimizes token embeddings with binary cross-entropy against masks. ConceptAttention is training-free at use time and therefore relies on the pretrained DiT objective rather than a new downstream loss. Mustafar trains a projector and multimodal stack with standard visual-instruction objectives, while its analysis phase uses image-text matching proxies based on pooled cross-attention maps rather than a dedicated CLIP-style contrastive loss. REPA uses feature-alignment regularization between diffusion hidden states and pretrained encoder outputs, and U-REPA adds a manifold loss to preserve relative sample geometry. A unified diffusion-to-CLIP objective family beyond fusion, BCE-style dense supervision, and feature matching has not yet stabilized [uncertain].
representation_target: The representation target is mainly local and compositional: object parts, attributes, action regions, viewpoint-sensitive structure, multi-view cues, spatial relations, and open-vocabulary masks. Several papers also expose a global descriptor role for some diffusion outputs, such as the 'register-like' shared tokens observed in Mustafar. Relative to plain CLIP, the aim is not just better global category separation but more faithful grounding of the text-relevant parts of the scene.
synthetic_regime: This route is primarily feature-transfer on real images rather than synthetic-only pretraining. Mustafar, ConceptAttention, DIFT, and most activation studies encode real images into diffusion latent space and extract features there. OVAM sits between real and synthetic regimes: it can generate pseudo-masks for synthetic images and also optimize class tokens from minimal supervision. In other words, diffusion is used more as a structured encoder than as a corpus generator in this auxiliary-representation line.
prompt_and_caption_source: Prompt sources are task dependent. OVAM uses a generation prompt plus a separate attribution prompt, with class names or open-vocabulary descriptors as optimized tokens. ConceptAttention uses simple concept words encoded by T5. Mustafar uses COCO captions for analysis and natural-language questions as task-aware prompts during supervised fine-tuning, explicitly probing whether the question can steer the feature extractor to relevant regions. Segmentation and matching papers also use benchmark labels, simplified class descriptions, and standard dataset captions rather than LLM-synthesized prompts as the dominant conditioning source.
data_scale_and_mix: Representative scales vary widely. Mustafar pretrains on the LLaVA-558K subset and fine-tunes on the LLaVA-Mix-665K SFT dataset, then evaluates on LLaVA-Bench, MMVP, BLINK-val, NaturalBench, and related sets. ConceptAttention evaluates on ImageNet-Segmentation (4,276 images), PascalVOC single-class (930 images), and PascalVOC multi-class (1,449 images). OVAM learns segmentation tokens with only a single annotation per class and reports pseudo-mask gains on synthetic images. There is no single, field-wide real/synthetic mixing ratio or canonical sample budget yet [uncertain].
filtering_and_quality_control: Quality control is mostly representation-centric rather than manual. Typical safeguards include averaging maps across multiple layers and timesteps, restricting extraction to empirically strong blocks, validating on hard compositional benchmarks, and in Mustafar explicitly mitigating prompt leakage by withholding text prompts during pretraining and using questions only during supervised fine-tuning. OVAM uses single-annotation token optimization to improve class-specific attention quality. Systematic human review, large-scale deduplication, or benchmark-contamination audits are rarely central in these papers [uncertain].
data_condensation_or_curriculum: Explicit sample curriculum is uncommon. What exists is mostly a representation-selection curriculum: choose the most useful blocks, timesteps, attention spaces, or alignment stages rather than selecting examples from a large synthetic buffer. Early-to-mid denoising steps and up-stage U-Net blocks are repeatedly preferred, and U-REPA effectively imposes a stage preference by aligning the middle U-Net representation instead of all blocks. A formal budgeted curriculum over synthetic samples is generally absent in this line [uncertain].
intervention_schema: The dominant intervention is semantic conditioning rather than pixel editing. Researchers alter the queried concept, class token, caption, or question prompt to inspect how the same image representation reorients around an object, part, attribute, action, background cue, or spatial relation. OVAM explicitly separates the generation prompt from the attribution prompt, while Mustafar swaps unconditional features for question-conditioned features to steer focus to task-relevant regions. This is closer to concept-level intervention inside the denoising pipeline than to full counterfactual image generation.
counterfactual_validity: These methods usually do not construct formal minimal counterfactual pairs, so counterfactual validity is only indirectly supported. Evidence comes from improved segmentation overlap, better matching on compositional benchmarks, and leakage analyses showing that text conditioning can sometimes overexpose prompt information. Strong claims about causal faithfulness, minimality of semantic changes, or identity preservation are therefore weakly supported in this sub-literature [uncertain].
set_structure_and_hardness_policy: Training is usually image-wise, but evaluation often uses deliberately hard pair or set structures. MMVP-VLM and Winoground provide visually similar yet compositionally distinct image-text pairs; BLINK probes visual prompting and spatial difficulty; semantic correspondence benchmarks compare source-target image pairs under pose, viewpoint, and occlusion changes. The methods themselves rarely train with explicit tuple-structured or curriculum hardness objectives, although the benchmark choice effectively stresses those capabilities.
shortcut_and_bias_probe: Bias probing is partial but meaningful. Mustafar directly evaluates on MMVP-VLM and Winoground to test whether diffusion-derived signals better capture viewpoint, structure, object presence, and compositional relations than CLIP. It also exposes a concrete shortcut risk: prompt leakage, where the downstream language model can recover the diffusion prompt instead of reasoning from the image. However, explicit generation of background or spurious-cue counterfactuals is not yet a standard component of this route.
temporal_supervision_details: Most evidence is image-based. DIFT shows that diffusion features can support temporal correspondence on DAVIS and JHMDB without video-specific fine-tuning, and ConceptAttention reports that the method generalizes to video generation, but the core CLIP-fusion papers in this bucket do not build a dedicated video-language training pipeline with frame-level supervision, edit propagation, or temporal consistency losses [uncertain].
video_anomaly_relevance: The relevance to video anomaly work is promising but still indirect. Diffusion cross-attention maps and early-timestep spatial features are attractive for frame-level abnormal cue localization, while DIFT-style temporal correspondence suggests a way to propagate these cues over time. Still, none of the representative papers directly evaluate weakly supervised video anomaly detection or FGCLIP-style temporal localization, so any transfer claim to anomaly pipelines remains forward-looking [uncertain].
evaluation_protocol: Evaluation is broad but fragmented. Representative protocols include zero-shot semantic segmentation, open-vocabulary mask generation, image-text matching as a proxy for spatial/compositional alignment, semantic correspondence, multimodal reasoning within LLaVA-style pipelines, and diffusion-training efficiency under representation alignment. The common pattern is to stress tasks that need dense localization or compositional discrimination rather than only global zero-shot classification.
datasets_and_metrics: Common datasets and metrics include ImageNet-Segmentation and PascalVOC with accuracy, mIoU, and mAP; MMVP-VLM and Winoground with compositional matching accuracy; BLINK-val, NaturalBench, and LLaVA-Bench for multimodal reasoning accuracy; COCO captions for attention-grounding visualizations; SPair-71k with PCK-style correspondence metrics in DIFT; DAVIS and JHMDB for temporal correspondence demonstrations; and ImageNet-256 with FID in REPA/U-REPA because those papers validate the semantic quality of aligned diffusion features through generative training behavior.
baselines: Baselines span both vision-language and diffusion interpretability families: OpenAI CLIP ViT-L/14 at 224 and 336 resolution, OpenCLIP ViT-H/14, SigLIP, DFN-CLIP, MetaCLIP, EVA-CLIP, DINO attention, TextSpan, transformer attribution methods for CLIP, DAAM on SDXL and SD2, raw Flux cross-attention, frozen CLIP-based LLaVA-v1.5-7B, and vanilla DiT/U-Net diffusion training without representation alignment. This baseline mix matters because many claimed gains are strongest on dense or compositional tasks rather than across every CLIP benchmark.
empirical_findings: Several consistent findings emerge. Up-stage U-Net queries and early-to-mid timesteps are usually the most transferable for fine-grained reasoning. OVAM shows that token optimization can raise pseudo-mask mIoU from 52.1 to 86.6 without retraining the base diffusion model. ConceptAttention shows that DiT attention output space is more transferable than raw cross-attention, achieving 71.04 mIoU on ImageNet-Segmentation and outperforming Flux raw cross-attention, DAAM, and strong CLIP interpretability baselines. Mustafar finds that diffusion cross-attention can exceed CLIP variants on spatial/compositional matching benchmarks, reports a +1.23% gain on BLINK-val from unconditional diffusion features, and improves MMVP by about +7 points over the original LLaVA-v1.5 baseline when cross-attention fusion is used. DIFT further supports the route by outperforming OpenCLIP and DINO on semantic correspondence, indicating that diffusion features carry discriminative local structure that contrastive embeddings often miss.
ablations: Ablations focus on where and when to read diffusion signals. Mustafar studies block choice, feature type (Cross-Q versus Out versus Res-Out), timestep, guidance strength, and fusion strategy. ConceptAttention compares attention spaces (cross-attention, value space, output space), concept update rules (cross only, self only, both), and raw Flux cross-attention against the full method. OVAM ablates token optimization and demonstrates that optimized open-vocabulary tokens improve several downstream diffusion-segmentation systems. U-REPA ablates alignment location and shows the U-Net middle stage plus manifold regularization works better than naive tokenwise alignment everywhere.
cost_normalized_utility: Compared with retraining a new large VLM, auxiliary diffusion features offer a favorable quality-to-intervention ratio, but they are not free. Extraction typically needs VAE encoding and one or more denoiser passes at selected timesteps, so inference is heavier than a single CLIP forward pass. Mustafar reports about 4 hours of pretraining and 10 hours of fine-tuning on 4 H100 GPUs for its multimodal stack, whereas OVAM's token optimization can finish in under a minute on one GPU. ConceptAttention adds little extra training cost because it is training-free, and REPA/U-REPA shift cost into training regularization while keeping inference unchanged.
synthetic_bias_and_leakage_audit: The clearest audited risk is leakage rather than classic synthetic bias. Mustafar shows that stronger text guidance can let the downstream language model recover the diffusion prompt, and mitigates this by removing text prompts during pretraining and delaying question prompts to supervised fine-tuning. OVAM and other attention-based pseudo-labeling methods also inherit whatever semantic and aesthetic biases are present in the underlying diffusion model and prompt vocabulary, but systematic audits for memorization, copyright leakage, or benchmark contamination are usually limited [uncertain].
limitations: The route is promising but immature as a CLIP-optimization recipe. Direct improvement of a reusable CLIP encoder is less developed than frozen-feature fusion or segmentation transfer. Gains are strongest on dense visual and compositional tasks, while CLIP can still remain better on instruction-heavy or broader world-knowledge benchmarks. Performance is sensitive to layer, timestep, guidance, and feature space choices. Extraction can be computationally expensive, and results from open U-Nets or Flux-style DiTs may not transfer cleanly to closed diffusion backbones. Video and anomaly evidence is still sparse.
relevance_to_current_project: This item is highly relevant. For CueBench and semantic counterfactual generation, OVAM- and ConceptAttention-style maps provide a concrete path to generate open-vocabulary region cues for objects, parts, actions, and abnormal evidence. For CLIPDiffusion and FGCLIP-style pipelines, the strongest immediate recipe is to extract up-stage cross-query or output-space features at early-to-mid timesteps, fuse them with CLIP tokens using lightweight cross-attention, and use the resulting maps as pseudo-region supervision. For video anomaly work, DIFT-like temporal correspondence and prompt-conditioned diffusion maps are plausible tools for propagating abnormal cues across frames, but they should be treated as exploratory until validated on anomaly benchmarks.
